Writing

Callouts

A callout is a blockquote that says what kind of thing it is. Put > [!type] on the first line and the quote becomes a coloured box with an icon — the same syntax Obsidian uses, and the same class names, so a vault written there looks like itself here.

You write

> [!note]
> Everything else in the quote is the body.

The type is case-insensitive: [!note], [!Note] and [!NOTE] are the same callout. (GFM's own alert syntax, which Clew also accepts, is stricter about this; Clew treats them all alike.)

Titles

Anything after the type becomes the title, and it may contain markdown — emphasis, code, even a [[wikilink]]. Without one, the callout is headed by the type as you wrote it, with a capital letter: [!CAUTION] is headed "Caution" and [!tldr] "Tldr", though they look like the types they stand for, a warning and an abstract (see the types). A type's own name gives its own title — [!note] and [!NOTE] are both "Note". (In 0.12.0 an untitled callout is always headed by its type's title: [!CAUTION] reads "Warning".)

You write

> [!tip] Titles can carry *emphasis* and [[links]]
> Body follows as usual.

Foldable callouts

Add - or + immediately after the type to make a callout collapsible. Both fold; the sign only decides how it starts.

You writeBehaviour
> [!note]Always open, not collapsible
> [!note]-Collapsible, starts collapsed
> [!note]+Collapsible, starts expanded

The mnemonic is slightly back-to-front: - does not mean "no callout", it means "start minimised". Click the title to toggle.

Why this matters beyond convenience Folding is native HTML <details>, not a script. So a foldable callout survives a live re-render while you type, works in a site exported from your vault with no JavaScript at all, and prints expanded — which is what you want on paper.

The types

Fifteen types, several answering to more than one name. Aliases are not merely tolerated: they resolve to the same callout, so [!tldr] and [!abstract] look the same; only an untitled one's heading tells them apart.

TypeAlso calledFor
note—A remark worth setting apart
abstractsummary, tldrThe short version
info—Context the reader may not have
todo—Something still to do
tiphint, importantAdvice worth taking
successcheck, doneIt worked
questionhelp, faqA question, or an answer to one
warningcaution, attentionMind this
failurefail, missingIt did not work
dangererrorThis will hurt
bug—A known defect
example—A worked case
quoteciteSomeone else's words
compatibility—Version or platform caveats
suggestion—An idea worth trying (not in 0.12.0)

Your own callout types

The fifteen are a starting set. Settings → Callouts defines more — a [!remark], a [!definition], a [!homework] — and changes the built-in ones. It has two lists. Global types are kept in Clew's own clew-settings.json and work in every vault on this machine; This vault's are kept in .clew/vault-settings.json and travel with the vault. Each row is one type:

Name
What you write between [! and ]: a letter, then letters, digits, - or _. Case does not matter, as with the built-in types.
Title
The heading a callout written with the type's name shows when it is not given one of its own; left blank, the name with a capital letter. Written with an alias, it is headed by the alias, as a built-in type is.
Icon
Any icon in Font Awesome Free, by name, chosen from a picker you can search. A plain name is looked for among the solid icons, then the regular ones, then the brands; regular: or brands: before the name picks the family.
Colour
A swatch, or typed: a hex value, rgb(), hsl() or a CSS colour name.
Aliases
Other names that open the same type, as [!tldr] opens an abstract — up to eight, separated by commas or spaces.

In .clew/vault-settings.json

"callouts": [
  { "name": "remark", "title": "Remark", "icon": "flask",
    "color": "#2e8b57", "aliases": ["rem"] }
]

The lists merge field by field: a built-in type, then a global definition, then this vault's, each overriding only the fields it sets. So a row named warning with nothing but a colour recolours the built-in warning and keeps its title and icon, and a vault can change a global type's colour without repeating its icon. Aliases add to a type's own. An alias that is itself a type's name is ignored; one that another type already has moves to this one, and a new type named like an existing alias takes the name — the row says so in each case.

As with the built-in types, one colour drives a custom callout's border, icon, title and tint, and Clew keeps it readable: a pale colour is darkened on the light theme and a very dark one lightened on the dark, so the same definition reads in both. Each row previews its callout in both themes. A row Clew cannot use — a name that is not a name, a colour that is not a colour, an icon Font Awesome does not have — says why and is skipped whole, never applied in part; that holds for a hand-edited file too, and a vault someone sent you can put nothing on the page but a title, a colour and an icon. Deleting a row takes two clicks.

Changes apply at once: the notes open in reading mode, live edit and embeds redraw, including after a hand edit of .clew/vault-settings.json. Each custom type gets a command in the command palette — Insert remark callout for the example above — and the editor toolbar's callout menu lists it. Custom types show wherever callouts do: reading mode, live edit, a website export, the reading-view PDF, and a note's HTML and LaTeX exports. (Not in 0.12.0.)

Caution — where a type travels A type in the Global list exists only on this machine: the same note opened on another computer shows it as an unknown type — a plain note-coloured callout, your colour and icon gone — so put a type the vault's notes depend on in This vault. And a vault kept in git carries its types only if .clew/vault-settings.json is committed — if your repository ignores .clew/, as the vaults chapter suggests for Clew's state, add that one file back. A synced folder (iCloud, Dropbox) carries it as it is.
Obsidian compatibility Obsidian defines extra callout types in CSS snippets; Clew does not read those definitions, and Obsidian does not read Clew's. A note using a custom type works in both only where both have it defined.

An unknown type

A type Clew does not recognise — neither built in nor one of your own — is still a callout, drawn as a note: the note's blue and its pencil icon, headed by the name as you wrote it with a capital letter ([!whatever] is headed "Whatever") or by the title you gave it. That is what Obsidian does, so a note using a type that only the other app defines still reads as a callout in both. Its data-callout is the name, in lower case, as in Obsidian. (In 0.12.0 an unknown type stays an ordinary blockquote, with the [!whatever] line visible as text.)

Admonition fences — the older spelling

Before Obsidian had callouts, vaults used the Admonition plugin, which writes fenced blocks instead of blockquotes. Clew reads those too, and renders them as the callouts they always meant — the same types, the same look:

You write (Admonition's syntax)

```ad-warning
title: Careful now
collapse: closed
The body, in ordinary markdown.
```

title: and collapse: (open / closed) are honoured; icon: and color: were the plugin's cosmetic overrides and the callout's own type styling applies instead. Without a title:, a fence is headed by its type as you wrote it, like an untitled callout: ad-hint is headed "Hint", though it looks like a tip, and ad-warning "Warning". (In 0.12.0 an untitled fence of a type Clew knows shows its icon and no heading.) An ad- type Clew's table does not know renders as a note titled with the raw type name, which is how the plugin treated user-defined types too.

Styling and compatibility

Each type has one accent colour, which drives its border, icon and title; the body keeps the page's own text colour, so a callout reads as emphasis rather than as a coloured slab. The background tint is mixed from that same colour, which is why callouts look right in both the dark and light themes without a second set of rules.

The markup carries both Obsidian's class names (callout, data-callout="note") and the jmarkdown engine's (markdown-alert). A CSS snippet written for Obsidian therefore keeps working in Clew — see Theming — and so does anything that targeted the engine's alert classes.

Icons are Font Awesome Free, embedded as inline SVG rather than fetched at render time, so they appear in reading mode, in an exported site, and on paper alike; a note's LaTeX export draws the same icon in its box.

Reference

You writeResult
> [!type]A callout of that type, headed by the type as written, capitalised: [!CAUTION] → Caution (in 0.12.0, the type's title)
> [!type] TitleThe same, with your title (markdown allowed)
> [!type]- / > [!type]+Collapsible, starting collapsed / expanded
> [!unknown]A callout drawn as a note, headed by the name written (in 0.12.0, an ordinary quote, the marker shown as text)
```ad-typeThe Admonition plugin's spelling of the same callout; untitled, headed by the type as written (in 0.12.0, no heading)
Settings → CalloutsYour own types, global or this vault's: name, title, icon, colour, aliases (not in 0.12.0)
callouts in clew-settings.json / .clew/vault-settings.jsonWhere those lists are kept; built-in < global < vault, field by field
